10300:
A malefactor is a person who does something wrong, harmful, or criminal. Simply put, it is someone who commits a bad act — whether that is a crime, a moral wrongdoing, or a harmful deed done against others.

Think of it this way: if you break something on purpose, you're doing a bad act. Now imagine that idea scaled up to real harm done to people or society — the person doing that harm is a malefactor.

The word has two built-in ideas packed into one:

  • A person — it always refers to a human being, not an event or a situation.
  • Who does wrong — the wrongdoing is active. They did something bad. They are not just a bad person in character; they committed a bad act.

This is an important distinction. A malefactor isn't just someone with evil thoughts. The word points to action — the actual doing of harm.

"Malefactor" covers a wide spectrum of wrongdoing. It doesn't lock you into only the most serious crimes. It can refer to:

  • A petty thief who steals from a shop
  • A corrupt official who takes bribes
  • A murderer or violent criminal
  • Someone who commits a serious moral wrong, even if not technically illegal

So whether the wrongdoing is minor or severe, the word can apply. However — and this is key — in practice, you'll most often see "malefactor" used for people who commit serious or meaningful wrongs, not trivial ones. You wouldn't typically call someone who jaywalked a malefactor. The word carries a sense of gravity.
The Tone and Register of the Word

This is a formal word. You will not hear it in casual everyday conversation. Instead, you'll encounter it in:

  • Legal or courtroom language
  • Formal writing and journalism
  • Literature, especially older or classic novels
  • Speeches, essays, and serious discussions about justice or morality

Because of this formal tone, "malefactor" carries a certain weight and seriousness. When someone uses this word, they are treating the wrongdoing as a matter of moral or legal significance — not something trivial.

Here are sentences ranging from simple to more realistic usage, so you can see the word in action:

  • "The police finally caught the malefactor who had been stealing from the market for months."
  • "The judge addressed the malefactor sternly before announcing the sentence."
  • "Society must find ways to rehabilitate malefactors, not simply punish them."
  • "The novel's hero dedicated his life to tracking down the malefactors who had wronged his family."
  • "Witnesses identified the malefactor from a lineup."
  • "The committee condemned the actions of the corporate malefactors who had defrauded thousands of investors."

Notice how in every sentence, the word points to a real person who did a real wrong — and the tone is always serious and formal.
How It Compares to Similar Words

You likely know other words that mean something similar. Here is how "malefactor" sits among them, so you can use the right word in the right context:

Criminal — refers specifically to someone who breaks the law. A malefactor can be a criminal, but "malefactor" also covers serious moral wrongs that may not be illegal. "Criminal" is more legal; "malefactor" is broader.

Wrongdoer — very similar in meaning, but simpler and more neutral in tone. "Wrongdoer" is the everyday, plain-English version of "malefactor."

Villain — used mostly in storytelling (movies, novels, folklore). A villain is a character who represents evil, often in a dramatic or narrative sense. "Malefactor" is more grounded in reality and real-world contexts.

Offender — common in legal and social work contexts. It is neutral and often used for people in the justice system. "Malefactor" is more literary and judgmental in tone.

Culprit — refers to the person who is responsible for a specific wrong or problem. "Culprit" focuses on who is to blame, while "malefactor" focuses on who did the wrong act.

Evildoer — strong, morally loaded word suggesting pure evil. "Malefactor" is a shade more neutral and precise; it doesn't always imply pure evil, just the doing of harm.

To sharpen the meaning further:

  • A malefactor is not someone who intends to do wrong but hasn't acted yet. The act must have happened.
  • A malefactor is not someone who accidentally causes harm. There is an implication of intent or at least willful neglect behind the wrongdoing.
  • A malefactor is not a neutral word. It carries moral judgment. When you call someone a malefactor, you are clearly identifying them as being in the wrong.

The plural is simply malefactors — referring to more than one person who commits wrongs.

"The town had long been terrorized by a band of malefactors."

If you ever need to remember this word quickly, hold onto this sentence in your mind:

A malefactor is a person who has done real harm or committed a serious wrong — described in a formal, weighty way.

It is the kind of word a judge, a novelist, or a philosopher might use — not because they want to sound fancy, but because the situation genuinely calls for precise, serious language about someone who has committed a meaningful act of wrongdoing.
10301:
Malefic means causing harm, evil, or misfortune — or having the nature or power to do so.

When you call something malefic, you're saying it is not just bad in a passive way, but that it actively works against wellbeing. It radiates harm. Think of it as describing a force, an influence, or a presence that is darkly destructive by its very nature.

Malefic is not a light word. It carries weight, shadow, and a sense of foreboding. It suggests something deeply sinister — not merely unpleasant or inconvenient, but genuinely threatening and harmful at its core.

It is also a formal, literary word. You would rarely hear it in everyday conversation. It belongs more naturally to writing, astrology, fantasy, poetry, or formal description where a precise, elevated word is needed to describe something as a source of evil or harm.

1. In Astrology (its most frequent home)

This is where you will encounter malefic most often. In astrology, planets are traditionally divided into two camps: benefic (good, helpful) and malefic (harmful, troublesome).

Mars and Saturn have long been called the malefic planets. The idea is that their influence over a person's life or a given moment brings hardship, struggle, conflict, or misfortune. A malefic planet in a bad position in your birth chart, astrologers say, signals difficulty.

2. In Literature and Fiction

Writers use malefic to describe a villain's gaze, a curse, a spirit, a power, or a force that is evil in nature and causes suffering.

"A malefic presence filled the room — something ancient and cruel, with no intention but harm."

3. In General Formal Description

Any person, thing, or force understood to cause harm through its very nature or influence can be called malefic. A corrupt regime's malefic grip on its citizens. A disease's malefic effect on the body. The malefic design of a trap.
How It Is Different from Similar Words

This is important, because malefic has close neighbors that overlap with it but aren't identical.

Malefic vs. Malevolent
Malevolent means wishing harm to others — it lives in the mind and the will. A malevolent person wants to hurt you.
Malefic is about causing or being capable of causing harm — it's about effect and nature, not just intention. Something can be malefic without being conscious or deliberately wishing harm (a cursed artifact, a destructive planet). So malefic is broader and more about inherent harmful power.

Malefic vs. Malicious
Malicious specifically implies deliberate, spiteful intent to cause harm — it is very focused on spite and choice.
Malefic does not require intent. It simply describes something as a source or agent of harm.

Malefic vs. Maleficent
Maleficent (an adjective you may know from the Disney character) means essentially the same thing — causing harm or doing evil. The two words are very close. However, malefic is more commonly used in astrology and technical or scholarly writing, while maleficent leans more literary. Malefic is also a bit more economical.

Malefic vs. Harmful / Dangerous
Harmful and dangerous are plain, everyday words. Malefic is far stronger and more loaded. It implies something darker than ordinary danger — an evil quality, an almost cosmic or sinister dimension of harm.

• "Ancient astronomers feared Saturn as the most malefic of all the planets, a cold, slow wanderer that presided over sorrow and limitation."
  • "The sorcerer's malefic spell drained the life from everything it touched."
  • "There was a malefic intelligence behind the attacks — calculated, cold, and entirely without mercy."
  • "She stared at him with a malefic calm that was more frightening than any outburst would have been."

The direct antonym of malefic — especially in astrology — is benefic, meaning bringing good fortune, help, or positive influence. Jupiter and Venus are the classic benefic planets, just as Mars and Saturn are the classic malefic ones.

Break it down mentally: male- relates to bad or evil (think malice, malevolent, malignant). The -fic part relates to making or doing (think terrific, horrific, prolific). So malefic essentially means evil-making or harm-doing — something that produces or embodies evil and harm. Once you see that pattern, it sticks.

Malefic describes something that causes harm, brings misfortune, or is evil in its nature or influence — a darkly powerful word used most often in astrology, literature, and formal writing to point to forces or things that are not just bad, but destructively and inherently so.
10302:
Maleficent means causing harm or evil, especially in a deliberate, active, or deeply wicked way.

When you call something or someone maleficent, you are saying that they don't just have the potential to cause harm — they actually do cause it, and there is a sense of moral wrongness, darkness, or wickedness attached to that harm.

Think of it this way: a sharp knife sitting on a table is dangerous, but you wouldn't call it maleficent. A sorcerer who deliberately casts a curse on a village to make its people suffer? That is maleficent. The word carries weight — it suggests evil with intention and force behind it.
What Makes It Different from Similar Words

This is where precision really matters. Several words seem close to maleficent, but each one means something slightly different:

  • Harmful is the most neutral of all. It simply means something causes damage. A thunderstorm is harmful. A virus is harmful. No moral judgment is implied — the thing just causes injury or loss.
  • Malevolent means wishing or desiring evil. It lives in the mind and heart of a person — it's about their intent, their attitude. A malevolent person wants bad things to happen to others, even if nothing bad has happened yet.
  • Malicious means deliberately intending to cause harm, often with a sense of spite or pleasure in doing so. It's about the conscious, mean-spirited decision to hurt.
  • Maleficent goes one step further than all of these. It is about actively doing or producing evil and harm. It combines the darkness of wicked intent with the actuality of harmful effect. Something maleficent doesn't just want to harm — it does harm, and it does so with a quality of deep, almost threatening evil. It's a stronger, more dramatic word than simply "harmful" or "bad."

In short:

  • Harmful → causes damage (no moral judgment)
  • Malevolent → wants evil (intent, no action required)
  • Malicious → deliberately acts to hurt (spite-driven)
  • Maleficent → causes/produces evil and harm, with a sense of wickedness and dark, active force

The adjective can describe a wide range of things:

  • People — A maleficent ruler who brings suffering to his people. A maleficent figure in a legend who destroys everything around them.
  • Forces or powers — A maleficent spirit, a maleficent supernatural energy, a maleficent curse.
  • Influences — A maleficent influence spreading through a community, corrupting and damaging it.
  • Actions or schemes — A maleficent plot designed to bring ruin to others.

The word fits best in contexts involving active evil — where something isn't passively dangerous but is working to cause harm, often with a dark or sinister quality.
The Tone and Register of the Word

Maleficent is a formal, literary word. You are unlikely to hear it in casual everyday conversation. You are more likely to encounter it in:

  • Literature, especially fantasy, mythology, or tales involving good vs. evil
  • Formal writing — essays, criticism, academic texts
  • Poetry or elevated prose
  • Stories involving magic, witchcraft, curses, or moral battles

Because of this, the word carries a slightly dramatic, elevated, even archaic flavor. When someone uses it, the effect is serious and weighty. It signals that the evil being described is not trivial — it is profound, active, and dark.

The word beneficent is its direct opposite, meaning doing good and causing good things to happen. If you ever want to remember maleficent, just remember: bene = good (like "benefit"), male = ill/bad (like "malady"). So beneficent is the do-gooder, and maleficent is the do-eviler.

Here are a few sentences that show the word being used naturally:

  1. "The tale warns of a maleficent force lurking in the deep forest, one that has claimed the lives of travelers for centuries."
    → A dark, active evil that kills — not just dangerous, but wickedly harmful by nature.
  2. "History has not forgotten his maleficent reign, during which thousands were imprisoned without cause."
    → His rule caused real, serious harm to people — it was actively wicked and damaging.
  3. "She believed the old woman to be maleficent, a presence that brought ruin to every household she entered."
    → The woman is described as a living cause of evil and misfortune.
  4. "The alchemist was warned against experimenting with maleficent substances that could corrupt both body and mind."
    → Substances that actively cause harm in a dark, dangerous way.

If you had to boil it down to its absolute essence:

Maleficent means actively causing harm or evil, with a quality of deep, intentional wickedness — it is a strong, formal, literary adjective used when you want to convey that something or someone is not merely dangerous, but genuinely, darkly, forcefully evil in its effects.
10303: Malevolence means a deep, deliberate desire to cause harm or suffering to others. It is not just disliking someone — it is actively wishing bad things upon them, or taking pleasure in their pain. It describes an attitude of ill will so strong that it becomes a defining feature of someone's character or behaviour.

Think of it in two parts: the wish and the willingness.

A malevolent person does not accidentally hurt others. They want to. They derive a kind of dark satisfaction from seeing others suffer, fail, or feel pain. This makes malevolence very different from, say, carelessness or anger. Anger is usually a reaction — hot, sudden, and often temporary. Malevolence is cooler, more deliberate, and often more lasting. It is not a burst of fury; it is a settled, deep-seated orientation toward harm.

Malevolence sits at the serious end of the spectrum of negative feelings. Consider this scale:

  • Irritation → mild annoyance
  • Resentment → holding a grudge
  • Spite → wanting to hurt someone because of a personal grievance
  • Malice → a firm intention to do harm
  • Malevolence → a broader, more fundamental disposition toward evil and harm

Malevolence is not petty. When you use this word, you are describing something deep and significant — not a bad mood or a minor grudge, but a genuine, often ingrained desire for harm.
Malevolence vs. Malice — a common confusion

These two words are closely related and are often used interchangeably, but there is a useful distinction:

Malice tends to be more specific and action-oriented. It usually refers to the intention behind a particular act — "He spread the rumour with malice." It is targeted.

Malevolence is broader and more about a general state of being or an attitude. It describes a person's character or outlook rather than a single act — "There was a deep malevolence in everything she did." It colours who someone is, not just what they did once.

In short: malice is often the tool; malevolence is often the personality behind it.
What it looks like in real life

Malevolence can show itself in many ways — subtle or obvious:

  • A powerful person who enjoys watching their employees fail and does nothing to help them
  • A character in a story who manipulates others not for any personal gain, but simply because they enjoy causing misery
  • Someone who, after a falling-out, quietly works to destroy another person's reputation over years

Notice that in all these cases, the harm is intentional, often calculated, and sometimes sustained. That is the fingerprint of malevolence.

The direct antonym of malevolence is benevolence — the desire to do good for others, to help, to bring wellbeing. The two words are mirror images. Where benevolence means "wishing good," malevolence means "wishing ill."

• "The villain's eyes were filled with malevolence as he planned his revenge."
  • "She sensed a quiet malevolence behind his polite smile."
  • "The regime's malevolence toward its own citizens was undeniable."
  • "His actions were not born of ignorance — they carried real malevolence."
Malevolence is a deep, deliberate desire to cause harm or suffering to others — not out of anger or accident, but out of a genuine, often coldly felt wish for evil.
10304:
Malevolent means having a deep, active desire to cause harm, pain, or suffering to others. A malevolent person doesn't just do harmful things by accident or out of anger in the moment — they want others to suffer. The desire itself is the heart of the word.

Think of it this way: if someone accidentally bumps into you and spills your coffee, that's not malevolent. If someone knocks your coffee over on purpose because they want your day to be ruined, and they feel pleasure doing it, that is malevolent. The key is the deliberate, deep-seated wish for harm.

Malevolent is a heavy, serious word. It sits at the darker end of the spectrum of "wanting bad things for others." You wouldn't use it to describe someone who was simply rude to you or cut you off in traffic. It implies something darker, colder, and more intentional — almost like evil is baked into a person's character or attitude.

Imagine a villain in a story who doesn't just want to win — they want the hero to suffer. They enjoy watching others in pain. That is a malevolent character. The word carries a sense of something sinister and deeply felt, not just a passing bad mood.
What Can Be Described as Malevolent?

This is where the word becomes very useful, because it isn't limited to just people.

A person can be malevolent — a malevolent ruler who takes pleasure in punishing citizens for no reason.

A look or expression can be malevolent — he gave her a slow, malevolent smile that made her feel unsafe.

A plan or intention can be malevolent — the scheme was entirely malevolent in design, meant only to destroy his rival's reputation.

A force or presence can be malevolent — in horror and fantasy, you'll often read about a malevolent spirit or a malevolent entity haunting a place. Here the word perfectly captures something that intends evil, not just something dangerous by nature (like a storm).

The common thread across all these uses: intention and desire to harm are present.
Malevolent vs. Words That Feel Similar

Understanding what makes a word different from its neighbors is one of the best ways to truly own it.

Malevolent vs. Mean: "Mean" is a mild, everyday word for unkindness. Someone who teases their little sibling is being mean. Calling that same person malevolent would be a dramatic overstatement. Malevolent is reserved for something genuinely dark.

Malevolent vs. Hostile: Hostile means unfriendly, aggressive, or openly opposed to someone. A hostile crowd boos a speaker. But hostile doesn't necessarily mean they wish deep harm — they might just want that person gone. Malevolent goes deeper; it implies a desire to see real suffering.

Malevolent vs. Wicked: Wicked usually describes actions or behaviour that goes against moral standards — a wicked deed, a wicked scheme. Malevolent, on the other hand, focuses more on the inner desire or disposition — it's about what someone wants deep inside.

Malevolent vs. Malicious: These two are the closest pair and are often used interchangeably. Both involve intent to harm. The subtle difference is that malicious tends to focus on specific harmful acts or intentions (he sent a malicious email to destroy her career), while malevolent often describes a broader, more pervasive, almost character-level quality of wishing harm (he was a malevolent presence in the office, slowly poisoning every relationship). Malevolent also fits supernatural or abstract descriptions more naturally.

The antonym of malevolent is benevolent. A benevolent person genuinely wants good things for others — they are kind, generous, and wish well for those around them. Knowing this pair makes both words stick far better in your mind. Wherever you see mal-, think "bad/evil." Wherever you see bene-, think "good/well."

Since you'll encounter this word's family in your reading and writing, here are the other forms:

Malevolence (noun) — the quality or state of being malevolent. "There was a cold malevolence in his eyes that everyone in the room could feel."

Malevolently (adverb) — in a malevolent way. "She stared at him malevolently as he walked away."

If you had to carry one sentence in your mind forever to remember what malevolent means, let it be this:

A malevolent person doesn't just do harm — they want to, they intend to, and on some level, they enjoy it.

It is a word for describing evil that is deliberate, deep, and conscious — whether in a real person's character, a supernatural force, or a cold, threatening expression. Use it when "mean" or "hostile" simply aren't dark enough, and when the desire to cause suffering is clearly at the centre of what you're describing.
10305:
Malfeasance means intentional wrongdoing by someone in a position of power or trust — particularly when that wrongdoing is illegal or a serious violation of their duties.

Think of it this way: someone is given authority, a role, or responsibility, and instead of using it properly, they deliberately use it to do something corrupt, dishonest, or harmful.

The two key ingredients are:

  • A person with power or an official role (a politician, judge, police officer, corporate executive, public official, etc.)
  • A deliberate wrongful act that abuses or violates that role

Malfeasance is not an accident or a mistake. It is an act the person knowingly chose to commit. If a government official accidentally approves the wrong contract, that is an error. If they secretly approve a contract in exchange for a bribe, that is malfeasance. The intent to do wrong is what makes it malfeasance.
Where You Will Hear This Word

Malfeasance is primarily a legal and formal term. You will encounter it in courtrooms, news reports about political scandals, corporate fraud cases, government investigations, and anywhere that involves official misconduct. It is rarely used in casual everyday conversation — it belongs to the formal, serious world of law, governance, and accountability.

Common phrases you will encounter:

  • "Malfeasance in office" — the most classic use; refers to a public official abusing their position
  • "Corporate malfeasance" — wrongdoing by company executives or leadership
  • "Official malfeasance" — misconduct by anyone in an official capacity
  • "Allegations of malfeasance" — accusations of such wrongdoing
  • "Guilty of malfeasance" — a finding of such wrongdoing in a legal context

• A mayor who accepts secret payments from a construction company in exchange for awarding them city contracts is committing malfeasance.
  • A judge who takes money to rule in favor of a particular party in court is committing malfeasance.
  • A police officer who deliberately plants false evidence on an innocent person is committing malfeasance.
  • A CEO who secretly moves company money into their own bank account is committing malfeasance.
  • A government health inspector who intentionally falsifies safety records for a restaurant that bribed them is committing malfeasance.

In each of these cases, notice the pattern: a person with authority, using that authority to deliberately do something corrupt or illegal.
The Spectrum of Related Legal Terms

Since malfeasance is a legal term, it exists alongside two related words that are worth knowing so you can fully understand where malfeasance sits:

Nonfeasance → Failing to do something you were required to do. Pure neglect or omission of duty. (Not doing what you should have done.)

Misfeasance → Doing something you were allowed to do, but doing it in a careless or improper way that causes harm. (Doing the right thing, but doing it wrongly.)

Malfeasance → Deliberately doing something illegal or clearly wrong while in a position of authority. (Doing what you should not do at all.)

A simple illustration: Imagine a building inspector.

  • They skip inspecting a building entirely → nonfeasance
  • They inspect it, but do a careless, rushed job and miss obvious problems → misfeasance
  • They knowingly certify a dangerous building as safe because the owner paid them off → malfeasance

Malfeasance is the most serious of the three because it involves deliberate, corrupt wrongdoing rather than negligence or omission.

One reason malfeasance is treated so gravely — legally and morally — is that it is a betrayal of trust. Society gives certain people authority precisely so they can serve, protect, or govern others. When those people weaponize that authority for personal gain or corrupt purposes, they are not just breaking a law — they are betraying the people who trusted them with that power. This is why malfeasance in office, for instance, can be grounds for removal from a position, impeachment, or criminal prosecution.
In a Sentence — How to Use It

• "The senator was investigated for malfeasance after it was discovered he had been taking kickbacks from lobbyists."
  • "The hospital board demanded an inquiry into the administrator's malfeasance."
  • "Years of corporate malfeasance finally came to light when a whistleblower released internal documents."
  • "He was removed from office on charges of malfeasance."
Malfeasance = a deliberate, wrongful act committed by someone in a position of power or official duty — an intentional abuse of authority, typically illegal or deeply unethical.
10306:
A malformation is an abnormal or irregular structure in something — most often a body part or organ — that came about because it did not develop or form the way it was supposed to. It is the physical result of something going wrong during the process of forming or growing. Think of it this way: when a structure is built or grows incorrectly, the flawed result is called a malformation.

The word always refers to a thing — a noun — meaning it points to the actual abnormal structure itself, not the process of it happening.

There are two ideas fused together in this word:

"Bad or wrong" + "the way something was formed or shaped" = a structure that formed badly or wrongly.

The critical word here is formed. A malformation is not just any problem. It is specifically a problem with structure — with the shape, arrangement, or physical construction of something. A malformation is not about how something behaves or functions (that would be a dysfunction). It is about how something is physically built or shaped.

That said, a malformation very often causes a dysfunction, because when something is built wrong, it usually does not work right either.

Here is the key checklist:

  • The structure exists in a form that is different from its normal, expected shape or arrangement.
  • This difference arose because the structure did not develop correctly — it was not formed right, right from the beginning.
  • It is not a result of injury or damage to something that was previously normal. If a bone breaks, that is not a malformation. But if a bone grew in the wrong shape from the start, that is a malformation.
  • The term usually implies a significant deviation from normal — not just a tiny variation, but something noticeably or meaningfully wrong.
Where Is This Word Used Most?

In Medicine (the most common context)

Malformation is used most heavily in medicine, especially when talking about the human body — particularly structures that did not develop correctly before or around birth.

Examples:

  • A heart malformation means the heart or one of its chambers, valves, or blood vessels did not form in the right shape. This is one of the most common types of birth defects.
  • A brain malformation means a part of the brain has an abnormal structure — for example, the two halves of the brain may not have separated properly, or a part of the brain may be missing or misshapen.
  • A skeletal malformation might mean a limb, a rib, or the spine has developed in an unusual or incorrect shape.
  • A vascular malformation refers to an abnormal formation of blood vessels — for instance, blood vessels that are tangled, oversized, or connected in a way they should not be.

The phrase congenital malformation is extremely common. "Congenital" means "present at birth," so a congenital malformation is an abnormal structure that a person is born with, having developed wrongly in the womb.

In Nature and Biology (outside the human body)

The word is not limited to human medicine. It also applies to animals and plants:

  • A bird born with a wing that did not grow into the correct shape has a wing malformation.
  • A plant that develops a stem or leaf in an abnormal structural form can be said to have a malformation.

In Engineering and Architecture (less common, but used)

Though rare, you can technically use malformation when describing non-living structures. A structure that was physically built or formed incorrectly — especially in a way that deviates significantly from its intended design — can be referred to as a malformation. However, in this context, people more often use words like "defect," "flaw," or "structural fault."

Malformations are not all equally serious. They exist on a wide spectrum:

  • Minor malformations — small structural differences that cause no major problems and may even go unnoticed. For example, a minor malformation of a toe that causes no pain or difficulty.
  • Major malformations — significant structural abnormalities that affect how a body part or organ functions, and may require medical treatment, surgery, or lifelong management. A serious heart or brain malformation would fall here.

While you did not ask for this, understanding causes gives the word much more meaning:

  • Genetic factors — errors or variations in a person's genes can cause structures to form incorrectly during development.
  • Environmental factors during development — exposure to harmful substances, infections, radiation, or certain medications during pregnancy can interfere with how a baby's structures develop.
  • Unknown causes — in many cases, doctors cannot pinpoint an exact reason why a malformation occurred.
  • Random developmental errors — sometimes, the complex biological process of forming a structure simply goes wrong by chance.
How Is This Word Used in Sentences?

Here are natural, realistic examples:

  • "The baby was born with a malformation of the heart that required surgery shortly after birth."
  • "The scan revealed a malformation in the brain that had likely been present since before birth."
  • "The surgeon specializes in correcting malformations of the spine in children."
  • "The colt had a leg malformation that prevented it from walking normally."
  • "Doctors discovered the malformation during a routine ultrasound in the third month of pregnancy."
  • "Not all malformations are visible from the outside — many are internal structural differences."
  • "The patient lived a full life despite the minor malformation found in her kidney."

Understanding nearby words will sharpen your understanding:

Malformed (adjective) — This is the describing form of the word. It describes something that has a malformation. "The child was born with a malformed ear."

Deformity — Very close in meaning, and often used interchangeably in everyday speech. However, strictly speaking, deformity tends to suggest a distortion or disfigurement — something bent, twisted, or warped out of its normal shape. Malformation specifically emphasizes that the structure was never formed correctly in the first place. In practice, especially in medicine, the two words often overlap significantly.

Anomaly — A broader word meaning simply "something that is unusual or different from normal." A malformation is a type of anomaly, but an anomaly does not have to be a malformation. An anomaly could be something unexpected in behavior, results, or data — not just physical structure.

Abnormality — Also a broader word meaning anything that deviates from the normal. A malformation is a physical structural abnormality, but not every abnormality is a malformation.

Defect — A very common synonym in medical and everyday usage. "Birth defect" and "congenital malformation" are often used to describe the same thing. However, "defect" has a slightly more general sense — it can refer to any kind of flaw (including functional flaws), while "malformation" is specifically structural.

A malformation is a physical structure — usually a body part or organ — that has an abnormal shape or form because it did not develop correctly. It is the name for the wrongly formed structure itself. The word is most at home in medical and biological contexts, particularly when discussing structures that were built incorrectly from the very beginning of their development. It differs from injury (which damages something that was once normal) and dysfunction (which is about performance, not shape). Malformations range from minor to life-altering, and they can affect any structure in a living thing.
10307:
A malfunction is when something stops working the way it is supposed to work.

More precisely: it is an instance of a device, system, machine, organ, or process operating incorrectly, improperly, or not at all — in a way that is different from how it was designed or expected to behave.

The word carries a built-in assumption: there is a correct, intended way this thing should work, and a malfunction is a departure from that. You cannot say a rock "malfunctioned." But you can say a rocket's engine did, because the engine was built with a specific, expected purpose.

A malfunction can take several forms:

  • Partial failure: The thing still works, but not fully or correctly. A keyboard malfunction where some keys stop responding is still a malfunction — the keyboard hasn't gone completely dead, but it no longer does its job properly.
  • Complete failure: The thing stops working entirely. A total power system malfunction leaves everything it was powering dark and dead.
  • Unpredictable behavior: The thing does something, but not what it is supposed to. A software malfunction might cause a program to open a wrong file, crash suddenly, or display scrambled data — it is "doing something," but doing it wrong.

The word applies across a wide range of domains:

Machines and technology: An engine malfunction, a sensor malfunction, a computer malfunction, a brake malfunction. These are perhaps the most common uses.

Software and digital systems: A software malfunction, a system malfunction, a navigation malfunction. Here it means the code or system is behaving incorrectly.

Biological systems and organs: A kidney malfunction, a thyroid malfunction, a heart malfunction. In medicine, it is used when an organ is not performing its biological role correctly — secreting the wrong amount of a hormone, filtering blood poorly, etc.

Processes and mechanisms: Even broader systems — like a safety protocol, a communication network, or an automated factory process — can experience a malfunction if they deviate from their designed operation.

A malfunction sits in the middle-to-serious range of severity, but it does not always mean total destruction. Think of it as a spectrum:

  • A minor malfunction: a small, perhaps temporary deviation. A flickering screen, a door sensor that sometimes fails to detect movement.
  • A serious malfunction: significant and potentially dangerous departure from normal function. A brake malfunction on a car. A reactor cooling system malfunction.

The word itself does not tell you exactly how bad things are — context does. But using "malfunction" signals that the problem is real and meaningful, not just a trivial inconvenience.
How to Use It in a Sentence

"The spacecraft experienced a malfunction in its navigation system, forcing mission controllers to take manual control."

"Doctors discovered a malfunction in the patient's immune system that was allowing infections to go undetected."

"A malfunction in the factory's assembly line caused production to halt for six hours."

"The pilot reported a malfunction before the emergency landing."

Notice the common verbs that pair with malfunction:

  • experience a malfunction
  • report a malfunction
  • cause a malfunction
  • suffer a malfunction
  • detect / discover a malfunction

And the common adjectives:

  • technical malfunction
  • mechanical malfunction
  • software malfunction
  • equipment malfunction
  • system malfunction
  • minor / major malfunction
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are close neighbors, but each has its own shade of meaning:

Malfunction vs. failure
A failure is often more absolute — it suggests something has completely stopped working or has collapsed entirely. A malfunction can be partial; the thing is misbehaving but may still be running in some form. A "heart failure" is a graver, more catastrophic event than a "heart malfunction," even though both are serious. In everyday use, though, they often overlap.

Malfunction vs. glitch
A glitch is typically minor and temporary — a brief, small hiccup that fixes itself or is easily corrected. A malfunction implies something more substantial and lasting. You would say your phone had a glitch if it froze for two seconds; you would say it had a malfunction if it can no longer make calls.

Malfunction vs. defect
A defect is a flaw that exists from the beginning — usually from the manufacturing or design stage. A malfunction can happen at any point in a device's life, including after it has been working correctly for years.

Malfunction vs. breakdown
A breakdown almost always implies complete, total cessation of function — the car broke down, meaning it stopped running entirely. A malfunction can be either partial or total, making it the broader of the two terms.

Malfunction vs. error
An error often refers to a mistake made by a person, or a specific incorrect value or action in a system. A malfunction refers to the broader failure of the system or device itself to operate correctly. Your GPS app might show an error (a wrong data point), but if the whole app freezes and cannot be used, that's a malfunction.

"Malfunction" is a fairly formal, technical-sounding word. You are more likely to see it in engineering reports, medical documents, news articles about accidents, official statements, and technical manuals than in casual conversation. When it appears, it signals seriousness — that something has gone wrong in a way worth investigating and correcting. It is a neutral, factual word; it describes a problem without assigning blame.

A malfunction (noun) is a specific occurrence of something — a machine, system, organ, or process — failing to work as it is designed or expected to. It can be partial or total, temporary or lasting, and spans everything from a faulty keyboard key to a failing human organ to a spacecraft navigation failure. It implies a known standard of correct operation, against which the failure is measured.
10308:
Malice is the desire to cause harm, pain, or suffering to someone — and crucially, doing so on purpose, with full awareness and intention.

It is not an accident. It is not a moment of rage. It is a cold, deliberate wish to see someone hurt, damaged, or destroyed. When someone acts with malice, they are not just angry — they want bad things to happen to a specific person (or people), and they may take steps to make that happen.

Think of it this way: if a rock falls and hits you, that's an accident. If someone throws a rock at you in a blind, unthinking fury, that might be anger. But if someone carefully plans to drop a rock on you at exactly the right moment because they want you to suffer — that is malice.

Malice always contains two things working together:

  1. Intent — the person means to cause harm. It is a choice, not a slip.
  2. Ill will — there is a hostile, negative feeling toward the target. They want the person to suffer, not just that they don't care whether the person suffers.

Both must be present. A surgeon who accidentally injures a patient has neither. A driver who runs a red light recklessly may intend the action (driving fast) but not the harm — still not malice. But someone who tampers with a colleague's work specifically to ruin their career? That is malice in full form.

It helps to draw clear lines:

  • Malice ≠ Anger. Anger is an emotion — it flares up and fades. Malice is more calculated and lasting. You can be furious at someone without bearing them malice. Malice often has a coolness to it; it can survive long after the heat of anger has passed.
  • Malice ≠ Hatred. Hatred is a feeling. Malice is the active desire to do something about that feeling — to see the person hurt. Hatred can sit inside you quietly; malice reaches outward.
  • Malice ≠ Indifference. Malice requires you to care enough about a person to want their suffering. Pure indifference — not caring whether someone is hurt — is not malice.
  • Malice ≠ Spite. These are close cousins, but spite is usually smaller in scale — a petty, almost childish desire to hurt someone as a reaction ("I'll ruin her party just to see her upset"). Malice is deeper, more serious, and more intentional. All spite has a touch of malice; not all malice is spite.

Malice is not always the same intensity. It can range across a spectrum:

At one end: A quiet, simmering wish that someone would fail — hoping bad things happen to a person you resent. This is malice in a passive sense. You haven't done anything yet, but the intention is there.

In the middle: Spreading false rumors about someone to damage their reputation, or sabotaging a coworker's project — deliberate harmful actions driven by that hostile intent.

At the far end: Taking careful, premeditated steps to cause serious harm to another person — physical, financial, or otherwise.

This is where the word carries its most precise and serious weight. In law, malice does not just mean "being mean." It has a very specific meaning that can determine whether someone is guilty of a crime and how severe the punishment is.

Malice in criminal law generally refers to the mental state of a person who commits a crime — specifically, that they intended to do harm or acted with reckless disregard for human life or safety.

"Malice aforethought" is a famous legal phrase. "Aforethought" means thought out in advance. So "malice aforethought" means the person planned the harmful act before doing it — they didn't just snap; they thought it through. This is central to defining murder (as opposed to manslaughter, which lacks this premeditated intent). When a prosecutor says a killing was done with malice aforethought, they are saying: the killer meant to kill, planned it, and was not acting out of sudden passion or accident.

There are also two subtypes in law:

  • Express malice: the person explicitly intended the harmful outcome (e.g., "I want to kill him" — and then they do).
  • Implied malice: the person didn't necessarily plan a specific harm, but acted in such a dangerously reckless way that the law treats it as if they intended the consequences (e.g., firing a gun randomly into a crowd — even without a specific target in mind, the recklessness implies malice).

In civil law (lawsuits between people, not criminal cases), malice matters too. For instance, in defamation cases (when someone lies about you and damages your reputation), proving that the person acted with "actual malice" — meaning they knew the statement was false or acted with reckless disregard for whether it was true or false — can be critical to winning the case and receiving higher damages.
Common Phrases and How They're Used

• "With malice" — done deliberately and with hostile intent. "He sabotaged her presentation with malice."
  • "Without malice" — done without any intention to harm; accidentally or innocently. "She criticized his work without malice — she just wanted to help."
  • "Bear malice toward someone" — to hold a persistent ill will or wish of harm against a person. "After all these years, she still bears malice toward her former business partner."
  • "Out of malice" — motivated purely by the desire to harm. "He spread those rumors out of malice, not because he believed them."
  • "Malice aforethought" — premeditated harmful intent (primarily legal; see above).
  • "With malice toward none" — a famous phrase from Abraham Lincoln meaning: without hostility or desire for revenge against anyone. It is often quoted to signal forgiveness or a generous spirit.
The Feeling of Malice from the Inside

If you try to imagine what malice feels like from the perspective of the person who holds it:

There is a target — a specific person (or group) they resent, fear, envy, or hate. And there is a want — a real desire to see that person fail, suffer, or be destroyed. It can feel almost like satisfaction in the idea of the other person's pain. Crucially, the person with malice is not indifferent — they are invested in the harm happening. They may plan, wait, and act carefully to ensure it does.

This is why malice is morally considered one of the darker human qualities. It is not impulsive or accidental — it is chosen.
Malice is the deliberate, intentional desire to cause harm or suffering to someone, driven by ill will — not accident, not impulse, but a cold and knowing wish that another person be hurt.
10309:
Malicious means having a strong, deliberate desire to harm, hurt, or cause damage to someone — and often taking pleasure or satisfaction in doing so.

If someone does something malicious, they are not acting by accident, not acting carelessly, and not acting with good intentions that went wrong. They are acting with the specific, conscious goal of causing pain, damage, or trouble to another person.

To truly understand this word, you need to see that it rests on three ideas working together:

1. Intent — the harm is on purpose.
This is the most important part. A person who accidentally knocks over your glass of water is not malicious. A person who deliberately knocks it over to ruin your work is. The word "malicious" is impossible without intention. The person chose to cause harm.

2. Ill-will — there is a dark feeling behind the act.
Malicious behavior doesn't come from a cold, neutral place. It comes from a place of spite, hatred, cruelty, or deep resentment toward someone. The person genuinely wants bad things for you. This inner feeling — this wish for someone to suffer — is called malice, and "malicious" is simply the adjective form of that noun.

3. A sense of pleasure or satisfaction in the harm caused.
A truly malicious person is not reluctant about the harm they cause. They often enjoy it, or at least feel deeply satisfied by it. This is what separates malicious behavior from, say, a difficult decision that hurts someone but is made out of necessity.
The Spectrum: What Is and Isn't Malicious

Understanding what a word does not mean is just as important as understanding what it does mean.

Not malicious:

  • A surgeon causes you pain during an operation. → The intent is to help you, not hurt you. Not malicious.
  • A driver accidentally hits another car. → It was an accident, not deliberate. Not malicious.
  • A manager gives you harsh feedback about your work. → If it's honest and well-meaning, not malicious — even if it stings.
  • A person lies to protect someone's feelings. → No desire to harm. Not malicious.

Malicious:

  • Someone spreads false rumors about you at work specifically to get you fired. → Deliberate, spiteful, harmful. Malicious.
  • A person secretly deletes your important files on a computer to sabotage your project. → Intentional damage with clear ill-will. Malicious.
  • A classmate mocks you in front of others not because it's funny, but because they want to see you feel humiliated. → Cruel intent. Malicious.

The key question to ask yourself is: "Did this person act this way because they wanted to cause harm?" If yes, it's malicious.

"Malicious" is not a light or casual word. It is strong and serious. It implies a real, deep wish to harm — not a moment of thoughtlessness or rudeness. When you call someone's actions malicious, you are making a significant claim: that they acted from a place of genuine ill-will, with full awareness of what they were doing.

This is why the word appears frequently in legal and formal contexts. In law, "malicious" is used to describe acts done with no legitimate reason, purely to cause harm — such as malicious prosecution (filing a lawsuit purely to harass someone) or malicious damage (deliberately destroying someone's property).

Malicious intent — the deliberate plan to cause harm. Courts often ask whether someone acted with malicious intent.

Malicious gossip — rumors or talk spread not out of curiosity but specifically to damage someone's reputation.

Malicious attack — an assault, whether physical or digital, carried out with the goal of causing serious harm.

Malicious software (malware) — computer programs designed specifically to damage, steal from, or take control of someone's system without their knowledge.

A malicious smile — a smile that is not warm or friendly, but rather one that signals the person is enjoying your misfortune or is plotting something harmful.

If you want to feel the meaning of this word rather than just know it intellectually, think of a villain in a story. Not a villain who does harm because they're desperate, or confused, or afraid — but one who enjoys causing suffering, who plans it, who delights in it. That quality — that dark, deliberate, pleasure-in-harm — is exactly what "malicious" captures.
Malicious = deliberately wanting to hurt or harm someone, driven by ill-will, and often with a sense of satisfaction in doing so.
